Snippet.Description:
Scherzo capriccioso may be the most uncharacteristic work ever written by Antonín Dvořák (1841–1904). When it premiered in May 1883 at the National Theatre in Prague, audiences were taken aback, wondering what had come over him. Critics speculated that he might be going through a personal crisis—never before had his music displayed such raw, dramatic intensity. This video presents a 2011 performance by the Lucerne Symphony Orchestra, conducted by Neeme Järvi at the Lucerne Culture and Congress Center.

Despite the title "Scherzo," which generally suggests a cheery and playful work, Dvořák’s Scherzo capriccioso in D-flat major, Op. 66, B. 131 embodies emotional lows — and is full of compositional mastery. Many presumed that depression, perhaps following the death of his mother in December 1882, or a midlife crisis may have triggered it. This otherwise highly productive phase also led to the creation of other major works such as the dramatic Symphony No. 7 and the Piano Trio in F minor.

The Scherzo capriccioso is marked by a sense of constant inner restlessness and agitation, even in its sonorous, idyllic passages. The score challenging for both orchestra musicians and conductor — it's a virtuosic tightly woven fabric of seemingly carefree, almost waltz-like tempos and dark, nearly grotesque accents (with echoes of Gustav Mahler). Added to this is a richly varied orchestration. Dvořák makes use of the tonal colors of instruments such as harp, bass clarinet, triangle, cymbals and tuba.

Neeme Järvi, born in 1937 in Tallinn, is the patriarch of a conducting family that includes his sons Paavo and Kristjan. After World War II, Estonia was absorbed into the Soviet Union, but a strong sense of national and cultural identity endured throughout the occupation. Järvi studied in Saint Petersburg, then known as Leningrad, before returning to Tallinn, where he played a key role in raising the country’s musical life to an international level as director of the opera house and the Estonian Radio Symphony Orchestra. From the 1980s onward, he has been an important advocate for Estonian culture abroad, helping bring the music of Arvo Pärt to major symphony orchestras in the West.

Text: Anastassia Boutsko

Snippet.Description:
2024 must have been the first time in [way too many] years that Furtwängler's Symphony No. 2 got a performance in Europe. It is fantastic that more people finally got to experience this epic work live. In the words of Dave Hurwitz, Furtwängler's 2nd is a "post-Brucknerian symphony that is a really fun work to listen to". Depends on your definition of "fun" of course (a typical performance lasts around 80 minutes), but it is indeed fascinating to hear how Furtwängler - a true symphonist - creates a whole sound universe out of nothing. For much of the first and last movement, Furtwängler takes a descending scale, takes an ascending scale, clashes them together, and turns this contraposition into music of incredible emotional depth. What's not to love about it?..

Snippet.Description:
Khatia Buniatishvili, Neeme Järvi and the Verbier Festival Orchestra perform Sergei Rachmaninoff’s Piano Concerto No. 3 in D minor, Op. 30 at the Verbier Festival in 2011.

Russian composer Sergei Rachmaninoff (1873 – 1943) wrote his third Piano Concerto in 1909 at the Ivanovka country estate 550 kilometers south east of Moscow. Rachmaninoff spent the summer months here from 1890 until his emigration to the US in 1917. The three movements of the piece recall the structure of typical solo concerts of the Romantic era. Piano Concerto No. 3 in D minor, Op. 30 was premiered by the New York Symphony Orchestra on November 28, 1909 in New York, conducted by Walter Damrosch. Rachmaninoff, who had been practicing the concert on a silent piano during his Atlantic voyage, played the solo part himself.

As a child, pianist Khatia Buniatishvili, born in 1987 in Tblisi, Georgia, was considered a wunderkind. She began to play the piano at the age of three and gave her first concert with the Tblisi concert orchestra at the age of six. International performances followed when she was ten. In 2008, she gave her US debut at New York’s Carnegie Hall. Since then, Buniatishvili has been regularly invited to many high-profile festivals and has given concerts in the world’s most renowned concert halls, for instance  at Vienna’s Musikverein, at the Concertgebouw Amsterdam and at the Berlin Philharmonic. She has won the highly respected Echo Classic Award twice.

The Verbier Festival is one of the most prestigious classical music events in the world. The quality of the participating artists as well as the originality of the programs have established the festival as a highlight of the music season. It takes place for two weeks in late July and early August in the mountain resort of Verbier, in Switzerland.
